claims.claim: Hobb says the reader drags the character's accumulated baggage through the reading.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Aidan Moher, A Dribble of Ink, 2007
claims.quote: he drags that same baggage through the reading

claims.claim: Hobb says she often had to trust the reader to make a leap the narrator did not make.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Aidan Moher, A Dribble of Ink, 2007
claims.quote: I often had to trust that the reader would make a leap
claims.page: Q on first vs third person

claims.claim: Hobb says she coped with first-person limits in Farseer by putting little prologues at the beginning of each chapter that gave the reader additional information.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Aidan Moher, A Dribble of Ink, 2007
claims.quote: little prologues at the beginning of each chapter
claims.page: Q on first vs third person

claims.claim: Hobb says there is a fairly clean dividing line between the Robin Hobb voice and the Megan Lindholm voice in her writing.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, Locus Magazine interview excerpts, December 2005
claims.quote: a fairly clean dividing line between the Robin Hobb voice

claims.claim: Hobb describes her own writing style as both leisurely and intimate.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: I would describe my writing style as both leisurely and intimate

claims.claim: Hobb says characterisation for her means putting in details and incidents that may not directly move the plot forward.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: details and incidents that may not directly move the plot forward

claims.claim: Hobb says the pacing at the beginning of any of her books is usually a lot slower than towards the end.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: The pacing at the beginning of any of my books is usually

claims.claim: Hobb attributes her slow openings to so many words being given over to character construction.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: so many words are given over to character construction

claims.claim: Hobb illustrates unearned consequence with a two-sentence summary of a friend killing a friend, saying it reads more like a joke than a devastating occurrence.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: That seems more like a joke than a devastating occurrence

claims.claim: Hobb says that when she propelled the reader directly into a scene without building up to it, the scene lacked the impact she wanted.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Robert Thompson, Fantasy Book Critic, January 2008
claims.quote: when I propelled the reader directly into it, it lacked the impact

claims.claim: Hobb says her story is really about how the events affect the characters rather than about the events themselves.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Patrick St-Denis, Pat's Fantasy Hotlist, 2005
claims.quote: how the events affect the characters rather than about the events

claims.claim: Hobb describes each sentence as narrowing an infinite number of possibilities down to a single track.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, interviewed by Patrick St-Denis, Pat's Fantasy Hotlist, 2005
claims.quote: With every sentence, you narrow an infinite number of possibilities

claims.claim: Hobb says some characters speak in longer sentences and some in shorter ones, as a way of differentiating them.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (Oct 2016), fan transcript at wetranscripts
claims.quote: Some characters speak in longer sentences, some speak in shorter sentences

claims.claim: Hobb says differentiating characters is a choice of vocabulary and a way of seeing things.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (Oct 2016), fan transcript at wetranscripts
claims.quote: it's a choice of vocabulary, it's a way of seeing things

claims.claim: Hobb gives her own household as an example of occupational vocabulary, where a sailor's galley, head and deck name the same rooms as her kitchen, bathroom and floor.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (Oct 2016), fan transcript at wetranscripts
claims.quote: we have a galley, we have a head, we have a deck
